RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria:
Haematuria is blood in the urine. Three questions frame it. (1) Is it really blood? — a positive dipstick needs red cells confirmed on microscopy; a positive dip with no red cells is myoglobin or haemoglobin, and red urine can be beetroot, rifampicin or menstrual contamination. (2) Visible or non-visible, painful or painless? (3) What is the source? — urological (tumour, stone, infection: clots, timing within the stream, colic) versus glomerular (dysmorphic red cells, red-cell casts, proteinuria, hypertension, AKI). The rule that carries the topic: painless visible haematuria in an adult is a urological cancer until proven otherwise (see bladder cancer, renal cell carcinoma), while a nephritic picture is a glomerulonephritis that can cost the kidneys in days (see glomerulonephritis).
🚨Two haematurias are emergencies. Painless visible haematuria — especially aged ≥45, a smoker or with aromatic-amine / dye exposure — is bladder / renal / upper-tract cancer until excluded → 2-week-wait referral for flexible cystoscopy + CT urogram (see bladder cancer). A nephritic picture — haematuria with proteinuria, hypertension and rising creatinine (± red-cell casts, dysmorphic red cells) — is a glomerulonephritis / rapidly progressive GN / vasculitis that can destroy nephrons within days → urgent nephrology and immunology (ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, see vasculitis, AKI). Also act on clot retention (catheter / irrigation) and an infected obstructed system (fever + loin pain + obstruction → emergency decompression).

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain:
Loin pain is pain in the flank / renal angle. The first split is renal / urological vs referred. Renal pain has renal-angle tenderness, urinary features (haematuria, dysuria, see haematuria) and often fever; referred pain comes from the musculoskeletal spine (movement-related), herpes zoster (dermatomal), the chest (basal pneumonia / pleurisy) or the gut. The next split is character: colicky loin-to-groin pain in a patient who cannot lie still is ureteric colic from a stone — its own topic (see loin-to-groin pain) — whereas constant, dull loin pain suggests infection, obstruction, a mass or a referred cause. Two emergencies hide here: an infected obstructed kidney and a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (see AAA).
🚨Two loin pains can kill. Fever + loin pain + an obstructing stone is an infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) — pus under pressure → emergency decompression (nephrostomy / stent) plus antibiotics, before rapid sepsis (see pyelonephritis, stone). A leaking / ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm presents as sudden flank / back pain + collapse or hypotension + a pulsatile mass in an older arteriopath — do not mistake it for renal colic → CT angiogram or straight to theatre (see AAA, pulsatile mass). And obstruction of a single / solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction causes AKI / anuria and needs urgent decompression (see AKI).

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin Pain:
Loin-to-groin pain is the classic presentation of ureteric colic — a stone passing down the ureter. It is sudden, severe and colicky (waves), and the patient is characteristically restless and writhing (unlike peritonitis, where they lie still). The pain radiates from the loin to the groin, and on to the scrotum / labia as the stone descends; a stone at the vesicoureteric junction adds bladder irritability (frequency, urgency). Most have haematuria (see haematuria) and vomiting. Confirm with a non-contrast CT KUB. This is a broad topic’s stone half (see loin pain): recognise the colic, but always exclude the mimics — a leaking AAA in the older patient (see AAA) and an ectopic pregnancy in a woman of reproductive age — and act on the infected obstructed stone and AKI.
🚨“Renal colic” is a diagnosis of exclusion in the wrong patient. A first episode over 60, or colic with hypotension or a pulsatile mass, is a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm until the aorta is imaged → CT angiogram, not a CT KUB (see AAA, pulsatile mass). In a woman of reproductive age, do a pregnancy test — an ectopic pregnancy presents as groin / iliac-fossa pain. Fever + an obstructing stone is an infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) → emergency decompression (nephrostomy / stent) + antibiotics (see pyelonephritis); and obstruction of a solitary or both kidneys causes AKI / anuria (see AKI).

1Recognise & exclude
🔍Recognise the colic
  • Sudden, severe, unilateral loin-to-groin pain in waves; the patient is restless / writhing (not still)
  • Radiation tracks the stone: loin → groin → scrotum / labia; a VUJ stone adds frequency / urgency
  • Usually haematuria and vomiting (see haematuria)
🚩Exclude the AAA
  • First colic over 60, hypotension or a pulsatile mass → a leaking AAA, not a stone
  • Image the aorta (CT angiogram) before accepting “renal colic” in an older arteriopath
  • A ruptured AAA is rapidly fatal if mislabelled (see AAA)
🚩Infected obstruction & AKI
  • Fever + an obstructing stone = pyonephrosis → emergency decompression + antibiotics (see pyelonephritis)
  • Obstruction of a solitary or both kidneys → AKI / anuria (see AKI)
  • These override the “wait for the stone to pass” approach
🟣Other mimics
  • Ectopic pregnancy: reproductive-age woman with iliac-fossa / groin pain → pregnancy test
  • Testicular torsion: acute scrotal pain, high-riding testis — examine the scrotum (see testicular torsion, acute scrotal pain)
  • Appendicitis / diverticulitis / biliary depending on side and site
🟢Stone facts that steer it
  • Size: <5 mm usually pass spontaneously; >10 mm rarely do
  • Site: the VUJ is the commonest place to lodge; also PUJ and the pelvic brim
  • Type: calcium oxalate (commonest), uric acid (radiolucent on X-ray, seen on CT), struvite (staghorn, infection), cystine
🩺Investigate
  • Urine dip (blood in ~90%, but absence does not exclude) + MSU; pregnancy test in women
  • Bloods: U&E / eGFR, calcium, urate, FBC / CRP
  • Non-contrast CT KUB is the gold standard; ultrasound in pregnancy / young patients

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria:
Dysuria is pain or burning on passing urine. Two questions sort it. (1) Internal or external? — internal dysuria (felt inside, throughout voiding) points to the bladder or urethra; external dysuria (stinging as urine passes over inflamed vulval skin) points to a vulvovaginal cause. (2) Where is the source? — bladder (cystitis / UTI: frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy urine), urethra (urethritis / STI: discharge, sexual history, see discharge), vagina (candida / other vaginitis), prostate (a man with fever and perineal pain) or the upper tract (pyelonephritis: fever + loin pain). The commonest cause is bacterial cystitis in a woman — but always consider an STI in the young / sexually active, and distinguish uncomplicated (a healthy non-pregnant woman) from complicated (men, pregnancy, children, catheter, recurrent, structural).
🚨Some dysuria is more than cystitis. Fever + loin pain + rigors is pyelonephritis / urosepsis → treat and consider admission (see pyelonephritis). A man with fever, perineal pain and a tender prostate has acute bacterial prostatitis — risk of retention; avoid vigorous prostatic massage and give a prolonged antibiotic course. Do not miss an STI — dysuria + urethral discharge is urethritis; screen, treat and arrange partner notification (see urethritis). Dysuria + visible haematuria in an older smoker needs a bladder-cancer work-up (see bladder cancer, haematuria). In pregnancy, treat even asymptomatic bacteriuria (with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic); in men and children, investigate the underlying cause.

🚩Upper tract & prostate
  • Pyelonephritis: fever + loin pain + rigors → treat, consider admission (see pyelonephritis)
  • Acute prostatitis (a man): fever, perineal pain, a tender boggy prostate, LUTS — retention risk
  • Avoid vigorous prostatic massage; prostatitis needs a prolonged antibiotic course
🟣Urethritis / STI
  • Younger / sexually active, often with urethral discharge (see discharge)
  • Chlamydia (commonest), gonorrhoea, Mycoplasma genitalium (see chlamydia, gonorrhoea)
  • Screen with NAAT, treat, and arrange partner notification (see urethritis)

  • Candida (itch, curdy white discharge, see candidiasis), trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary Tract:
Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) are the cluster of bladder-emptying and bladder-storage complaints. The organising split is storage (irritative) — frequency, urgency, nocturia, urgency incontinence — versus voiding (obstructive) — hesitancy, a weak / intermittent stream, straining, terminal dribbling and incomplete emptying — plus post-micturition dribble. That split targets the cause and the treatment: voiding LUTS in an older man is usually benign prostatic hyperplasia (see BPH), while storage LUTS suggests an overactive bladder or bladder irritation (UTI, stone, cancer). A DRE and urinalysis anchor the assessment (see prostate on DRE). Throughout, screen for the red flags: visible haematuria (cancer, see haematuria), retention (see acute / chronic) and a neurological cause.
🚨LUTS can hide serious disease. Visible haematuria with LUTS is bladder or prostate cancer until excluded (see bladder cancer); persistent irritative symptoms in a smoker can be carcinoma in situ. Chronic retention (a painless, palpable bladder with a high residual, overflow incontinence and a rising creatinine) is obstructive uropathy → catheterise / decompress (see chronic retention); acute retention is painful and needs immediate catheterisation (see acute retention). Cauda equina presents with LUTS plus saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms and faecal incontinence → emergency MRI (see cauda equina). A hard, nodular prostate, bone pain or a raised PSA points to prostate cancer (see prostate cancer).

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary Retent:
Acute urinary retention is the sudden, painful inability to pass urine, with a palpable, tender, distended bladder. It contrasts with chronic retention, which is painless and high-volume (see chronic retention). The commonest cause is benign prostatic hyperplasia in an older man (see BPH), usually with a precipitant — constipation, a new drug (anticholinergic, opioid, decongestant), a UTI, alcohol or recent surgery. The immediate job is to relieve it: catheterise and record the residual volume drained, then find and treat the cause (see urinary retention). Always screen for the emergencies: cauda equina and high-pressure retention with AKI.
🚨Relieve first, then think. Insert a urethral catheter immediately (a suprapubic catheter if urethral fails) and record the residual volume (typically 500–1000 mL; relief of pain confirms it). Cauda equina presents as retention with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms, back pain and faecal incontinence → emergency MRI and surgery — do not simply catheterise and discharge (see lower back & spine). High-pressure retention (bilateral hydronephrosis, a raised creatinine) risks post-obstructive diuresis after decompression — monitor urine output and U&E and replace fluids (see AKI). Clot retention (heavy haematuria) needs a 3-way catheter and irrigation, not a standard catheter (see haematuria).

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urinary Rete:
Chronic urinary retention is painless, gradual, incomplete bladder emptying with a large post-void residual (often over a litre). It is painless because the bladder stretches slowly — the opposite of the painful, palpable, tender bladder of acute retention (see acute retention). The critical split is pressure: low-pressure chronic retention has a compliant bladder and normal kidneys, whereas high-pressure chronic retention transmits pressure up the ureters → bilateral hydronephrosis, renal failure and nocturnal enuresis — the dangerous one. The commonest cause is BPH (see BPH); also prostate cancer, urethral stricture and a neurogenic bladder. Confirm with a bladder scan and always check renal function and a renal-tract ultrasound (see urinary retention).
🚨High-pressure chronic retention is a renal emergency in slow motion. Bilateral hydronephrosis + a raised creatinine + nocturnal enuresis (bed-wetting in an adult man) means high-pressure chronic retention → catheterise and expect a post-obstructive diuresis — the patient can lose litres, so monitor urine output and U&E and replace fluids; watch for decompression haematuria (see AKI, CKD). Do not rush a trial without catheter here — it often needs long-term drainage or definitive surgery. Overflow (dribbling) incontinence from a palpable bladder is retention, not a primary incontinence — treat the bladder, not the leak (see incontinence). And exclude an underlying malignancy or neurological cause.

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incontinence:
Urinary incontinence is the involuntary leakage of urine. The whole approach is to classify the type, because that drives the treatment. Stress incontinence leaks on effort (cough, sneeze, exercise) from a weak sphincter / pelvic floor; urgency incontinence is a sudden urge then a leak from an overactive bladder (detrusor overactivity, see bladder & urodynamics); mixed is both. Overflow incontinence is dribbling from a chronically full bladder — it is really retention (see chronic retention); continuous leakage suggests a fistula or ectopic ureter; and functional incontinence is a normal tract in someone who cannot reach the toilet. Always screen for reversible causes (DIPPERS) and the red flags. A bladder diary, urinalysis and post-void residual anchor the work-up.
🚨Not all leakage is “just incontinence.” Continuous dribbling — especially after childbirth, pelvic surgery or radiotherapy — is a vesicovaginal fistula (or an ectopic ureter) and needs referral. Overflow from a palpable bladder with a high residual and renal impairment is chronic retention — treat the bladder, not the leak (see chronic retention). New incontinence with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms or back pain is cauda equina → emergency MRI (see lower back & spine). And incontinence with visible haematuria earns a bladder-cancer work-up (see haematuria).

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / Anuria:
Oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr, roughly <400 mL/day) and anuria (near-zero, <50–100 mL/day) are usually the presentation of acute kidney injury (see AKI). Classify by the AKI triad: pre-renal (hypoperfusion — the commonest and most reversible), renal / intrinsic (acute tubular necrosis, interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis, rhabdomyolysis), and post-renal (obstruction — bladder outlet, bilateral ureters, or a blocked catheter). Anuria in particular flags obstruction, a blocked catheter or a vascular catastrophe. The first, cheapest steps are to exclude a blocked catheter and assess volume status; the two things to treat immediately are hyperkalaemia and fluid overload.
🚨Check the catheter, then the potassium. A blocked catheter is the commonest cause of ward “anuria” — flush or replace it first. Hyperkalaemia is the immediate killer in AKI → ECG (peaked T waves, broad QRS) and emergency treatment (calcium gluconate, insulin–dextrose, salbutamol). Fluid overload / pulmonary oedema in an anuric patient may need dialysis (see renal replacement therapy). Post-renal obstruction is reversible — a bladder scan and renal ultrasound (hydronephrosis) then decompress (catheter / nephrostomy, see retention, stones). Know the urgent-dialysis criteria (AEIOU): refractory Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalaemia), Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia (pericarditis / encephalopathy).

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Polydipsi:
Polyuria is a genuinely high urine volume (>3 L/day), usually with compensatory polydipsia (thirst). First separate true polyuria (large volumes) from frequency (small volumes passed often, a lower-urinary-tract symptom, see LUTS). Then split the mechanism: osmotic diuresis (a solute drags water out — commonest is diabetes mellitus with glycosuria, so check the glucose first, see diabetes) versus water diuresis (a problem with ADH — diabetes insipidus: cranial lacks ADH, nephrogenic is kidney-unresponsive, see diabetes insipidus), plus primary polydipsia (excess intake). Hypercalcaemia and hypokalaemia also cause polyuria. The classic pathway is glucose → U&E / calcium → osmolalities → a water deprivation test.
🚨Check the glucose before anything clever. Diabetes is the commonest cause; polyuria + polydipsia + weight loss + ketones is DKA — an emergency (see DKA), and profound hyperglycaemia with dehydration in an older patient is HHS (see HHS). Hypercalcaemia — polyuria with confusion and “bones, stones, abdominal groans” — needs treating (malignancy / hyperparathyroidism, see hypercalcaemia). Cranial diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery or a head injury produces massive dilute urine and risks hypernatraemia — monitor sodium and fluid balance. Lithium is a classic cause of nephrogenic DI.

1Triage & screen
🔍True polyuria vs frequency
  • True polyuria = >3 L/day of urine; frequency = small volumes passed often (see LUTS)
  • A bladder diary (frequency-volume chart) settles it
  • Then split osmotic (solute-driven) from water (ADH) diuresis
🚩Diabetes mellitus (glucose first)
  • Glycosuria → osmotic diuresis + thirst; often weight loss
  • DKA (ketones, type 1, see DKA) / HHS (older, type 2, profound dehydration, see HHS)
  • Check a capillary / venous glucose immediately (see type 1, type 2)
🟣Diabetes insipidus
  • Cranial: lack of ADH (pituitary surgery, tumour, trauma) — responds to desmopressin
  • Nephrogenic: kidney unresponsive to ADH (lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, CKD) — no response to desmopressin
  • Both give dilute urine despite a rising plasma osmolality (see diabetes insipidus)
🟣Primary polydipsia & electrolytes
  • Primary (psychogenic) polydipsia: excess water intake, dilute urine, low-normal plasma osmolality
  • Hypercalcaemia causes polyuria (nephrogenic-DI effect) — treat it (see hypercalcaemia)
  • Hypokalaemia also impairs urinary concentration
🟢Drugs & other
  • Diuretics, lithium, SGLT2 inhibitors, alcohol / caffeine
  • CKD (impaired concentrating ability, see CKD)
  • Post-obstructive diuresis and the recovery phase of acute tubular necrosis
🩺Investigate & the deprivation test
  • Glucose (first), U&E, calcium, potassium; plasma + urine osmolality
  • Water deprivation test then desmopressin: primary polydipsia concentrates on deprivation
  • Cranial DI concentrates only after desmopressin; nephrogenic DI concentrates with neither
Glucose first, then think ADH. Confirm true polyuria, then rule out diabetes mellitus (glucose) and hypercalcaemia (calcium). If those are normal, the water deprivation test separates primary polydipsia from cranial and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
